description: The Sun is a G-type main-sequence star, the yellow dwarf at the gravitational heart of the Solar System and the yardstick against which every other star here is measured. It is seeded at the origin because the whole map is heliocentric: distances, brightnesses and radii are all quoted relative to it (R☉, L☉, M☉). About 4.6 billion years old and roughly halfway through its hydrogen-burning life, it fuses some 600 million tonnes of hydrogen every second at a core temperature near 15 million K. It has no constellation of its own — from Earth it appears to drift along the ecliptic through the zodiac over the course of a year.

Proxima Centauri is the closest star to the Sun, a diminutive red dwarf about 1.30 parsecs (4.25 light-years) away in the constellation Centaurus. Its name is simply Latin for 'nearest', and it is the outermost, gravitationally bound third member of the Alpha Centauri system, orbiting the bright A–B pair once in roughly 550,000 years. Barely a seventh the mass of the Sun and thousands of times fainter, it is a UV Ceti-type flare star whose brightness can jump dramatically when magnetic outbursts erupt from its surface. It hosts at least one planet, the roughly Earth-mass Proxima b, which orbits within the star's habitable zone — making it the nearest known exoplanet to Earth.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Alpha Centauri A, the Sun-like G2V primary; SIMBAD 'alf Cen A' lists no Gaia DR3 row (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Alpha Centauri is the nearest stellar system to the Sun and, at apparent magnitude near zero, the third-brightest star in the night sky. What the eye sees as a single point is really a close binary of two Sun-like stars — the G2 primary Rigil Kentaurus (component A) and the slightly cooler K1 dwarf Toliman (component B) — orbiting each other every 80 years, with the red dwarf Proxima as a distant third companion. Component A is almost a twin of our own Sun in mass, temperature and colour, which makes the system a favourite target for imagining nearby habitable worlds. Its estimated age is debated, with determinations ranging from roughly 5 to 8 billion years.

Barnard's Star is a faint red dwarf in Ophiuchus and, after the Alpha Centauri system, the closest individual star to the Sun. It is famous for having the largest proper motion of any known star: measured by E. E. Barnard in 1916, it races across our sky at more than 10 arcseconds a year, covering a full lunar diameter roughly every 180 years. An ancient, metal-poor star perhaps 10 billion years old, it is too dim to see without a telescope despite its proximity. Decades of planet-hunting finally paid off in 2024–25 with the confirmation of several sub-Earth-mass planets circling it.

Wolf 359 is one of the smallest and faintest stars known in the Sun's immediate neighbourhood, a cool red dwarf in Leo just under 2.4 parsecs away. With barely a tenth of the Sun's mass and about a thousandth of its luminosity, it sits close to the lower limit of how small a hydrogen-fusing star can be. It is a UV Ceti-type flare star (catalogued as the variable CN Leonis), prone to sudden brightenings driven by intense magnetic activity. Its proximity has made it a fixture of science fiction, most famously as the site of a pivotal battle in Star Trek: The Next Generation.

Lalande 21185 is a red dwarf in Ursa Major, catalogued from the star charts of the 18th-century French astronomer Jérôme Lalande. Although still far too faint for the naked eye, it is the brightest red dwarf in the northern sky and one of the closest stars to the Sun at about 2.5 parsecs. Roughly 40% of the Sun's mass and an old star some 8 billion years old, it shows the high proper motion typical of nearby stars. Precise radial-velocity monitoring has revealed at least two planets orbiting it, both more massive than Earth.

gaiaDr3Note: Sirius A; SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source among its identifiers (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Sirius, the Dog Star of Canis Major, is the brightest star in the night sky, blazing at apparent magnitude −1.46 — a distinction it owes both to its intrinsic luminosity and to its closeness, just 2.6 parsecs away. Its name comes from the Greek Seirios, meaning 'scorching' or 'glowing', and its heliacal rising once marked the flooding of the Nile for the ancient Egyptians. The bright star we see is Sirius A, a hot blue-white A-type star about twice the Sun's mass; it is orbited every 50 years by Sirius B, a faint but extraordinarily dense white dwarf that was the first such star ever discovered. Together with Procyon and Betelgeuse, Sirius forms the Winter Triangle.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents the Luyten 726-8 system, resolved to primary component A (BL Ceti / GJ 65 A); the companion is UV Ceti.
description: Luyten 726-8 is a close binary of two nearly identical red dwarfs in Cetus, about 2.7 parsecs away, discovered by the prolific proper-motion cataloguer Willem Luyten. Both stars are tiny, cool M dwarfs near the bottom of the main sequence, and both are vigorous flare stars. Its component B, UV Ceti, is the prototype of the entire class of UV Ceti-type flare stars — dwarfs that can brighten by a magnitude or more in seconds during magnetic eruptions. Component A carries the variable-star name BL Ceti and is the one whose position anchors this entry.

Ross 154 is a nearby red dwarf in Sagittarius, one of the many high-proper-motion stars catalogued by the American astronomer Frank Elmore Ross in the 1920s. Lying about 3 parsecs from the Sun, it is a young, magnetically active M dwarf and a UV Ceti-type flare star, carrying the variable designation V1216 Sagittarii. Its flares are frequent, with major outbursts separated on average by only a couple of days. With less than a fifth of the Sun's mass, it shines at barely four-thousandths of the Sun's luminosity.

Ross 248 is a faint red dwarf in Andromeda, another discovery from Frank Ross's proper-motion surveys, sitting about 3.2 parsecs away. It is a small, cool M dwarf whose brightness varies slightly as star-spots rotate across its face, earning it the BY Draconis-type variable name HH Andromedae. Its chief claim to fame lies in the future: because it is moving toward the Solar System, in roughly 36,000 years Ross 248 will briefly become the closest star to the Sun, displacing the Alpha Centauri system for several thousand years. The Voyager 2 spacecraft is loosely headed in its general direction.

Epsilon Eridani, formally named Ran, is a young orange K-type dwarf in the constellation Eridanus and one of the closest Sun-like stars, about 3.2 parsecs away and easily visible to the naked eye. Younger and cooler than the Sun, it is magnetically active and encircled by at least one debris disk, a dusty analogue of our own asteroid and Kuiper belts. Its proximity and Sun-like character made it a target of Project Ozma, the first modern search for radio signals from other civilisations, back in 1960. A confirmed giant planet, Epsilon Eridani b (named AEgir), orbits within the system.

Lacaille 9352 is a red dwarf in Piscis Austrinus, catalogued by the 18th-century French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille during his survey of the southern sky. At about 3.3 parsecs it is among the nearest stars, and with roughly half the Sun's mass it is one of the brighter, more massive red dwarfs in the solar neighbourhood. It has the fourth-highest proper motion of any known star, sweeping across nearly seven arcseconds of sky each year. A quiet, comparatively bright M dwarf, it hosts a compact family of confirmed planets, one of which lies in its habitable zone.

Ross 128 is a nearby red dwarf in Virgo, discovered by Frank Ross and lying about 3.4 parsecs from the Sun. Although catalogued as the flare star FI Virginis, it is unusually quiet and magnetically settled for a red dwarf, a sign of its middle age. In 2017 it drew attention as the host of Ross 128 b, a roughly Earth-mass planet in a temperate orbit — at the time the second-closest known Earth-size world beyond the Solar System. Its relatively calm activity makes that planet a comparatively promising place to look for benign conditions.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents the EZ Aquarii triple system, resolved to primary component A (GJ 866 A).
description: EZ Aquarii is a remarkable triple system of red dwarfs in Aquarius, about 3.5 parsecs away, also catalogued as Luyten 789-6. Its three stars are all tiny, cool M dwarfs; two of them orbit each other in a tight inner pair every eleven days, with the third circling that pair every few years. The whole system is a UV Ceti-type flare star, prone to sudden magnetic brightenings, and carries the variable name EZ Aquarii. Because its components are so low in mass and luminosity, the entire system is far too faint to be seen without a telescope despite its closeness.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents 61 Cygni A (K5V), the primary of this wide binary; component B is a cooler K7 dwarf.
description: 61 Cygni is a wide binary of two orange K-type dwarfs in Cygnus, about 3.5 parsecs away, and holds a special place in the history of astronomy. In 1838 Friedrich Bessel used its large parallax to make the first successful measurement of the distance to any star beyond the Sun, earning it the nickname 'Bessel's Star'. Its exceptional proper motion had already flagged it as a nearby object; Giuseppe Piazzi called it the 'Flying Star'. Today it remains the star with the highest proper motion still visible to the unaided eye, its two components orbiting each other over roughly 680 years.

gaiaDr3Note: Procyon A; SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source among its identifiers (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Procyon is the brightest star in the small constellation Canis Minor and the eighth-brightest in the entire night sky, at apparent magnitude 0.34. Its name comes from the Greek for 'before the dog', because it rises just ahead of Sirius, the Dog Star, as the sky turns. Like Sirius, it is a bright, nearby star with a white-dwarf companion: Procyon A is a yellow-white F-type star beginning to swell as it exhausts its core hydrogen, orbited every 40 years by the faint Procyon B. It forms the third vertex of the Winter Triangle alongside Sirius and Betelgeuse.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Struve 2398 A (GJ 725 A), the primary of a red-dwarf binary; both components are flare stars.
description: Struve 2398 is a binary of two red dwarfs in Draco, about 3.6 parsecs away, named for the entry it holds in the double-star catalogue of Friedrich Georg Wilhelm von Struve. Both stars are modest M dwarfs of similar size, orbiting their common centre of mass over several centuries. Each is a flare star, subject to the sudden magnetic brightenings common among active red dwarfs. This entry stands for the brighter primary, component A (also known as GJ 725 A), which anchors the pair's position on the sky.

gaiaDr3Note: Represents Groombridge 34 A (GX Andromedae / GJ 15 A), the primary of a red-dwarf binary; both components are flare stars.
description: Groombridge 34 is a pair of red dwarfs in Andromeda, about 3.6 parsecs away, taken from a star catalogue compiled by the English astronomer Stephen Groombridge in the early 19th century. Its two components, the flare stars GX Andromedae and GQ Andromedae, are both small, dim M dwarfs invisible to the naked eye. The brighter primary, component A (GJ 15 A), hosts at least two confirmed planets, including a super-Earth in a short orbit. This entry represents that primary, which fixes the system's place on the sky.

gaiaDr3Note: Resolved to Epsilon Indi A (HD 209100), the K-dwarf primary; the system also contains a brown-dwarf binary (Ba/Bb).
description: Epsilon Indi is a nearby orange K-type dwarf in the southern constellation Indus, about 3.6 parsecs away and comfortably visible to the naked eye. Smaller and cooler than the Sun, it is a relatively quiet star notable for its rich retinue of companions. Circling the main star at a great distance is a pair of brown dwarfs, Epsilon Indi Ba and Bb — one of the closest known brown-dwarf systems to the Sun. A giant planet, Epsilon Indi Ab, several times the mass of Jupiter, was later confirmed on a wide, long-period orbit.

Tau Ceti is a single G-type star in Cetus, about 3.65 parsecs away, and the closest solitary Sun-like star to the Solar System after Alpha Centauri A. Slightly smaller and cooler than the Sun and notably poor in heavy elements, it is an old, stable, magnetically calm star — qualities that have long made it a touchstone in the search for life. In 1960 it was one of the two original targets of Project Ozma, and it recurs throughout science fiction as a plausible destination. It is surrounded by a substantial debris disk, and several planet candidates have been proposed, though none is yet unambiguously confirmed.

Kapteyn's Star is a red subdwarf in the southern constellation Pictor, about 3.9 parsecs away, discovered in 1898 by the Dutch astronomer Jacobus Kapteyn. It is the closest known halo star to the Sun — an ancient, metal-poor member of the Milky Way's Population II — and it orbits the Galaxy backwards, retrograde to the disk's rotation, probably having been stripped from a dwarf galaxy long ago. When discovered it held the record for the highest proper motion of any star, later surpassed by Barnard's Star. At around 11 billion years old, it is one of the oldest stars in the solar neighbourhood.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD 'Altair' lists no Gaia DR3 source among its identifiers (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Altair is the brightest star in the constellation Aquila, the Eagle, and one of the nearest bright stars at just over 5 parsecs; its name comes from an Arabic phrase meaning 'the flying eagle'. A hot white A-type star, it forms the southern vertex of the Summer Triangle together with Vega and Deneb. Altair spins extraordinarily fast, completing a rotation in under nine hours, which flattens it into a visibly oblate spheroid whose equator is more than a fifth wider than its poles. In 2007 it became the first main-sequence star other than the Sun to have its surface directly imaged, revealing that flattening and the temperature difference between its cooler equator and hotter poles.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD 'Vega' lists no Gaia DR3 source among its identifiers (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Vega is the brightest star in the constellation Lyra and the fifth-brightest in the night sky, a hot blue-white A-type star about 7.7 parsecs away. It served for over a century as the anchor of the photometric magnitude scale, the star against which the brightness of others was defined at magnitude zero. Because of the slow precession of Earth's axis, Vega was the northern pole star around 12,000 BCE and will be again in roughly 13,700 CE. Like Altair it is a rapid rotator, seen nearly pole-on, and it was one of the first stars found to be surrounded by a dusty debris disk — the archetype of the 'Vega-like' disks.

gaiaDr3Note: Fomalhaut A; SIMBAD lists no Gaia DR3 source among its identifiers (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Fomalhaut is the brightest star in Piscis Austrinus, the Southern Fish, and a lonely beacon of the autumn sky often called the 'Solitary One' because it has few bright neighbours; its name derives from Arabic for 'the mouth of the fish'. A young, hot A-type star about 7.7 parsecs away, it is encircled by a strikingly sharp-edged ring of dusty debris that has made it a showcase for studies of planetary systems in formation. An object imaged within that ring, Fomalhaut b, was hailed as one of the first exoplanets seen directly in visible light, though later observations showed it to be an expanding cloud of debris from a colossal collision rather than a planet.

gaiaDr3Note: SIMBAD 'Pollux' lists no Gaia DR3 source among its identifiers (saturated bright-star hole).
description: Pollux is the brightest star in Gemini and, despite its Beta designation, outshines its neighbour Castor; the two mark the heads of the mythological twins the constellation is named for. It is an orange giant about 10 parsecs away, a star that has exhausted the hydrogen in its core and swollen to nearly nine times the Sun's diameter. That makes it the nearest giant star to the Solar System. In 2006 it became one of the first giant stars confirmed to host a planet — Pollux b, later formally named Thestias — a gas giant a few times the mass of Jupiter.
